description: We’re EDES Orbit, a team focused on space exploration, engineering, and technology. Our interests include AI, software, hardware, data, satellites, the Moon, and human exploration. We’re looking for teammates with skills in coding, web development, graphic design, data analysis/visualization, AI/ML, hardware, design, and communication who want to build creative solutions together.
summary:
Where Earth Got Darker is a website for finding real trends in NASA Earth data. Pick a variable measured by a NASA satellite or produced by a NASA model, and a globe shows where it changed since 2001, how fast, and whether the change is statistically significant. Click any 1 degree square to see its year-by-year record. Statistical tests decide which squares get color, with a correction for testing tens of thousands of squares at once.

Our case study asks where Earth now reflects less sunlight. We wrote down five hypotheses before opening any data and ran three. From 2001 to 2025, 11.3% of Earth’s surface shows a significant trend toward reflecting less sunlight. Earth as a whole absorbed more sunlight, +0.89 W/m2 per decade from March 2000 to May 2026, as we predicted. Our tests linking clear-sky reflection to aerosol came out inconclusive over East China and against our prediction over India, and we show both. The Compare page sets satellite against model and uses k-means machine learning to group places that changed alike.

Sunlight that Earth stops reflecting is absorbed instead, adding heat, so it matters where reflection is falling and how sure we can be.
details:
Where Earth Got Darker is a website for finding real trends in NASA Earth data. Pick a variable, such as sunlight reflected by Earth (CERES) or aerosol from a satellite (MODIS) or a model (MERRA-2), and a globe shows where it changed since 2001, how fast, and whether the change is statistically significant. Grey squares have no significant trend. Click any square to see its year-by-year record.

A Python pipeline tests every 1 degree cell for a trend and corrects for testing about 64,000 cells at once, so chance alone doesn’t color the map. The website only reads those results, so it needs no server or sign-in.

Our case study asks where Earth now reflects less sunlight. We wrote down five hypotheses before opening any data, ran three, and report every result, including a miss over India. We also wrote a paper on it. The Compare page sets a satellite record beside the model and uses k-means machine learning to group places that changed alike. Detective Cases has visitors make their own prediction before they see the evidence.

We want people, students especially, to see the difference between a change and a change that stands out from noise, and to see that an honest test can fail. Along the way we accounted for changes in the satellite instruments, labeled model data as a model, and never said a trend was “caused by” anything.

We built it with Python (xarray, NumPy, SciPy, Numba), TypeScript, React and d3-geo, and host it on GitHub Pages. Claude Code helped write the code and other AI models reviewed it. Our full AI disclosure is in the repository.
